observation.visible_scene: Top-down view of a plain white surface. A right hand at the right edge grips the end of a long line of dark, glossy metallic spheres (magnetic balls). At the start the spheres form two single-file chains that diverge leftward from the hand, creating an open V / two arms (an upper arm running near-horizontally to the left edge and a lower arm angling down-left).
visible_changes: Over the first ~0.8 s the two-arm V configuration is essentially held steady, with only very slight settling of the chains.

From about t=0.93 s onward the upper arm progressively bends down and folds alongside the lower arm, converting the single-file V into a parallel double-row strip; this merge begins at the hand side and the joining front travels leftward across the frame.
The open V angle at the left shrinks continuously as more of the upper arm is brought into alignment with the lower arm.
Around t=1.4–1.6 s the two remaining diverging tails at the far left converge and join the double row, completing a uniform two-row strip spanning the frame.
From roughly t=1.6 s to the end of the clip the double-row strip is static; the hand remains fixed at the right holding its end, and the spheres show no further rearrangement.
The specular highlights on the spheres move with the spheres (surface reflections), not as separate objects.
outside_clip_unknowns: How the two arms were originally arranged or formed before this segment.
What happens after the clip ends (whether the strip is further folded, separated, or moved).
Whether the hand actively feeds/folds the chain or simply holds one end while the rest shifts.
The exact material and the mechanism (manual pulling vs. magnetic self-alignment) producing the fold.
uncertain_details: The precise driver of the leftward-moving merge front is not visible; only the geometric change is observable.
Very small shifts of the chains in the early static interval are hard to attribute to motion vs. camera/hand jitter.
A possible fingertip briefly appears at the extreme left edge in a couple of frames, but its role is unclear.
Background gives no reliable evidence of camera motion, so the camera is treated as stationary.
